betterCitation: Audre Lorde, The Cancer Journals, The Transformation of Silence into Language and Action, a paper of December 1977 (1980)
reason:
REFUTED on two grounds, and the evidence that refutes it is the very document the verifier cites.

GROUND ONE, THE EDITION WAS NEVER OPENED. The evidence block names Sister Outsider: Essays and Speeches, The Crossing Press, 1984. I downloaded the PDF at the URL given and extracted it with pdftotext. Its own headnote, the first thing on the page, says: This speech by Audre Lorde was originally delivered at the Lesbian and Literature panel of the Modern Language Association's December 28, 1977 meeting. It was then published in many of Audre's books, including “The Cancer Journals” and “Sister Outsider.” ... This is the full text of the version appearing in “The Cancer Journals,” published 1980 by spinsters press. So the text read is the Cancer Journals setting of 1980, not the Crossing Press setting of 1984, and the evidence block's sentence about which edition was consulted is not true of the document it links. The sentence itself is genuine and correctly transcribed, and I read it in context: I was going to die, if not sooner then later, whether or not I had ever spoken myself. My silences had not protected me. Your silence will not protect you. But under this month's standard the wording has to exist in the NAMED edition, and the named edition is the one nobody looked at. For a four-word sentence the risk of drift between the two printings is small, which is exactly why this kind of slip survives a verifier; it is still a citation asserting something that was not checked.

GROUND TWO, AND THIS ONE IS FATAL RATHER THAN FIXABLE. The brief puts speeches and oratory out of scope, on the Makers' ground. The piece is a speech. The source document calls it a speech in its first four words; Lorde's own volume is subtitled Essays and Speeches and this is one of the speeches, carrying in the book a headnote giving the panel, the city and the date; it was delivered aloud before it was ever printed. The proposal tags it Essay, and the gate asks whether the tag is the form of the work. It is not. The closed vocabulary has no tag that fits a delivered paper, which is itself the sign that this belongs to the other year. Note also that the note field is empty: it says nothing about the delivery, nothing about which printing was read, nothing about the volume's subtitle. A line with this much to disclose cannot ship with a blank note.

WHAT I DID NOT FIND AGAINST IT. The attribution is not in doubt, the line is famous in the exact sense the brief allows (it is the sentence the piece is known by), it is publishable as it stands, shipped.js returns shipped empty, near empty, audre lorde at 0 of 3, not banned, and it would have helped the month's women count and its theme. That is precisely why it got this far. If the owner rules that a conference paper printed in a prose collection counts as an essay and not as oratory, then it must ship on the text that was actually read, with the delivery disclosed in the note, and the betterCitation field carries that source line (121 characters, leads with the name, no dash). Until that ruling, it is out.
